title: Air Strider port to Unreal Engine: I spent one week bringing my dream game to UE 5.8. The biggest breakthrough was animation.
author: Chilkus
selftext:
A few days ago i posted about the game I dreamed about as a kid that I prototyped in a couple of weeks using AI today I can show you the game running in Unreal Engine!

**Air Strider** is a mixture of Desert Strike, Ace Combat and Robotech/Macross. You switch between Fighter, Strider and Mech, each with its own role, movement and space in the battlefield.

The inspiration goes back to that scene where Max meets Miriya at the arcade. Watching their game go from 2D to 3D in the ’80s blew my mind. 🤯

(The attached video shows the **Unreal version**. You can play the **original browser version** here:  
[https://chilkus.itch.io/air-strider](https://chilkus.itch.io/air-strider))

**Porting the gameplay was surprisingly straightforward.**

The core gameplay, missions, dialogue and other systems were already defined in the browser version. Bringing them into Unreal went pretty smoothly.

The thing that really changed the project was getting a transforming model properly animated.

I modeled a temporary VF-1 lookalike and manually posed its three forms.   
Then, with AI handled the rigging and animation work, those three poses became something I could actually watch transform in motion. The design is a placeholder, but it let me explore the experience I had in my head.

Seeing the parts move into place made an enormous difference. Suddenly, flying between buildings, transforming mid-flight and dropping into the streets felt much closer to that childhood fantasy.

**The animations started influencing the gameplay.**

Once I could see the transformations properly, it felt natural to improve how the game moved through them: how one form flows into another, how the camera follows, and how you arrive back in combat.

That was probably the most interesting part of the process. Improving the presentation gave me a clearer sense of how the gameplay should feel, which encouraged more changes to both.

Then I started pushing the rest of the visuals:

* **Lumen, improved post-processing and more stable anti-aliasing** made the game shine almost immediately.
* **Asset-store vegetation and rocks** gave the environments more detail and variety.
* **Explosion VFX** made combat more satisfying.
* **Niagara** let me tweak smoke and other effects to better fit the game.
* **Chaos-based destruction** gave me better-looking destruction that also performed better in my implementation.
* **GPU and CPU performance is twice as fast!**
* **(don't tell anyone yet but it runs in multiplayer too!!!)**

Each improvement made the next one more tempting. Better transformations deserved better camera work. Better environments deserved better explosions. And those explosions really needed to leave some damage behind 😅

For me, the best implication of AI game development is how much more of the process I can participate in. I could model something, pose the forms I wanted, and use AI to help get through the rigging and animation work needed to bring it into the game. Also, the thing moves so fast that you spend a great part of the process actually playing your game which is critical to iterate and polish. 

The browser version let me build and play the idea quickly. Moving to Unreal helped me discover how much further I could to take it.

Any help spreading the word is appreciated!   
I'll be more diligent replying any questions comments you may have this time :)
